claims.source: Despite success with cancer immunotherapies, approved immunotherapies are not available for the majority of cancer patients and only a minority of treated patients realize a durable response (Haslam and Prasad, 2019; Ben-Aharon et al., 2018; Darvin et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Haslam and Prasad, 2019; Ben-Aharon et al., 2018; Darvin et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Only a minority of treated patients realize a durable response to immunotherapies.
claims.source: Despite success with cancer immunotherapies, approved immunotherapies are not available for the majority of cancer patients and only a minority of treated patients realize a durable response (Haslam and Prasad, 2019; Ben-Aharon et al., 2018; Darvin et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Haslam and Prasad, 2019; Ben-Aharon et al., 2018; Darvin et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2023).

claims.claim: Not all tumors with high indel mutational loads respond to checkpoint inhibitors.
claims.source: While many studies correlate tumor insertion and deletion (indel) mutation load with immunotherapeutic response, not all tumors with high indel mutational loads respond to checkpoint inhibitors (Mandal et al., 2019; Turajlic et al., 2017; Yarchoan et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2019; Van Allen et al., 2015; Samstein et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2022; Rizvi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Mandal et al., 2019; Turajlic et al., 2017; Yarchoan et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2019; Van Allen et al., 2015; Samstein et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2022; Rizvi et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The typical adult solid tumor contains a median of 54 coding somatic nucleotide variants.
claims.source: The typical adult solid tumor contains a median of 54 coding somatic nucleotide variants, many of which have the potential to create novel neoantigens or Mutation-Associated NeoAntigens (ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020; Vogelstein et al., 2013; Segal et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020; Vogelstein et al., 2013; Segal et al., 2008).

claims.claim: Approximately 5% of mutations are insertions/deletions (indels) or splice site changes that alter the open reading frame of the transcript.
claims.source: Approximately 5% of mutations are insertions/deletions (indels) or splice site changes that alter the open reading frame of the transcript (ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020; Vogelstein et al., 2013; Segal et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium, 2020; Vogelstein et al., 2013; Segal et al., 2008).

claims.claim: Nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) plays an important role in messenger RNA (mRNA) quality control and normal gene expression.
claims.source: In normal cells, nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) plays an important role in messenger RNA (mRNA) quality control, as well as normal gene expression (Frischmeyer and Dietz, 1999; Mendell et al., 2004; Carrard and Lejeune, 2023; Sun and Chen, 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Frischmeyer and Dietz, 1999; Mendell et al., 2004; Carrard and Lejeune, 2023; Sun and Chen, 2023).

claims.claim: NMD may aid immuno-evasion in cancer cells by eliminating RNA transcripts from genes that carry truncating mutants.
claims.source: In cancer cells, however, NMD may aid immuno-evasion by eliminating RNA transcripts coming from genes that carry truncating mutants (Nogueira et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Nogueira et al., 2021).

claims.claim: Knockdown of the NMD pathway with siRNA enhances the anti-tumor immune response.
claims.source: Previous work has shown knockdown of the NMD pathway with small interfering RNA (siRNA) enhances the anti-tumor immune response (Pastor et al., 2010; Castle et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Pastor et al., 2010; Castle et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Loss of UPF1 showed increased levels of aberrant transcripts and mutant proteins in alleles targeted by NMD.
claims.source: Analysis of cell lines with loss of the UPF1 RNA helicase and ATPase gene (UPF1), a key mediator of NMD degradation, also showed increased levels of aberrant transcripts and mutant proteins in the alleles targeted by NMD (Oka et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Oka et al., 2021).

claims.claim: There is no report of a specific chemical inhibitor of the NMD pathway with good bioavailability.
claims.source: Despite early studies showing little toxicity with NMD inhibition, there is as of yet no reports of a specific chemical inhibitor of the pathway with good bioavailability (Martin et al., 2014; Durand et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2022; Gotham et al., 2016; Gopalsamy et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Martin et al., 2014; Durand et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2022; Gotham et al., 2016; Gopalsamy et al., 2012).

claims.claim: A high-throughput assay was created to query the effects of a curated library of small molecules on NMD function.
claims.source: In this work, we create a cell-based high-throughput assay to query the effects of a curated library of small molecules on NMD function.
claims.evidence: Described as work performed in this study.

claims.claim: A lead compound capable of inhibiting NMD was identified from the screen.
claims.source: From this screen, we identify a lead compound capable of inhibiting NMD and ascertain its protein target as nonsense-mediated mRNA decay-associated phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)-related kinase (SMG1), a kinase that is a critical mediator of NMD.
claims.evidence: Described as work performed in this study.

claims.claim: The protein target of the lead compound is SMG1.
claims.source: From this screen, we identify a lead compound capable of inhibiting NMD and ascertain its protein target as nonsense-mediated mRNA decay-associated phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)-related kinase (SMG1), a kinase that is a critical mediator of NMD.
claims.evidence: Described as work performed in this study.

claims.claim: A specific and bioavailable small molecule inhibitor of SMG1 (KVS0001) was designed.
claims.source: As the lead compound produced unacceptable toxicity in animal models, we then designed a specific and bioavailable small molecule inhibitor of SMG1 (KVS0001) that is well-tolerated in vivo.
claims.evidence: Described as work performed in this study.

claims.claim: KVS0001 is well-tolerated in vivo.
claims.source: As the lead compound produced unacceptable toxicity in animal models, we then designed a specific and bioavailable small molecule inhibitor of SMG1 (KVS0001) that is well-tolerated in vivo.
claims.evidence: Described as work performed in this study.

claims.claim: Targeted inhibition of SMG1 by KVS0001 leads to the presentation of novel neoantigens identifiable by T-cells.
claims.source: We then demonstrate that targeted inhibition of SMG1 by KVS0001 leads to the presentation of novel neoantigens identifiable by T-cells leading to tumor growth inhibition in vitro and in vivo.
claims.evidence: Described as work performed in this study.

claims.claim: Targeted inhibition of SMG1 by KVS0001 leads to tumor growth inhibition in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: We then demonstrate that targeted inhibition of SMG1 by KVS0001 leads to the presentation of novel neoantigens identifiable by T-cells leading to tumor growth inhibition in vitro and in vivo.
claims.evidence: Described as work performed in this study.

claims.claim: Two genes, STAG2 and TP53, did not express their expected proteins when assessed by western blots or immunohistochemistry.
claims.source: Through evaluation of this panel, we discovered two genes, Stromal Antigen 2 (STAG2) and Tumor Protein p53 (TP53), which did not express their expected proteins when assessed by western blots (STAG2) or immunohistochemistry (TP53) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The absence of STAG2 and TP53 proteins was suspected to be due to NMD because the inactivation was the result of frameshift mutations.
claims.source: Because the inactivation of these two genes was the result of frameshift mutations, we suspected that the absence of the proteins was due to NMD.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the observation of frameshift mutations and protein absence.

claims.claim: Whole transcriptome RNA-sequencing supported the suspicion that the absence of STAG2 and TP53 proteins was due to NMD.
claims.source: This suspicion was supported by whole transcriptome RNA-sequencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Cook et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and cited work (Cook et al., 2022).

claims.claim: STAG2 RNA transcripts decreased by 20-fold on average relative to wild-type transcripts in the parental cell lines.
claims.source: Notably, we saw an average decrease of STAG2 RNA transcripts by 20-fold and TP53 by 6-fold relative to their respective wild-type transcripts in the parental cell lines.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data from the study.

claims.claim: TP53 RNA transcripts decreased by 6-fold on average relative to wild-type transcripts in the parental cell lines.
claims.source: Notably, we saw an average decrease of STAG2 RNA transcripts by 20-fold and TP53 by 6-fold relative to their respective wild-type transcripts in the parental cell lines.
claims.evidence: Supported by RNA-sequencing data from the study.

claims.claim: Treatment with emetine demonstrated up to a 60-fold recovery of mutant RNA transcript expression.
claims.source: Treatment with the canonical protein synthesis inhibitor emetine, working indirectly to inhibit NMD, demonstrated up to a 60-fold recovery of mutant RNA transcript expression, establishing this panel as appropriate for HTS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Carter et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citation (Carter et al., 1995).

claims.claim: A next-generation sequencing (NGS) assay for NMD was designed.
claims.source: We then designed a next-generation sequencing (NGS) assay for NMD (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Described as work performed in this study and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The three cell lines were mixed in equal proportions and plated in 96-well plates followed by treatment with one compound per well.
claims.source: We mixed the three cell lines in equal proportions and plated the mixture in 96-well plates followed by treatment with one compound (drug) per well.
claims.evidence: Described as experimental method in this study.

claims.claim: NMD inhibition efficacy was determined by comparing wild-type and truncating mutant transcript expression levels in a ratiometric manner.
claims.source: We determined NMD inhibition efficacy by comparing the wild-type and truncating mutant transcript expression levels in a ratiometric manner.
claims.evidence: Described as experimental method in this study.

claims.claim: The wild-type sequences of the reciprocally knocked out clone served as internal references.
claims.source: Specifically, the wild-type sequences of the reciprocally knocked out clone (i.e., wild-type STAG2 sequence from the TP53 knockout clones, and wild-type TP53 sequence from the STAG2 knockout clones) served as internal references, providing a ratiometric assay of mutant to wild-type transcript abundance.
claims.evidence: Described as experimental method in this study.

claims.claim: The ratiometric assay minimized confounders introduced by nonspecific transcriptional activators or generally toxic agents.
claims.source: This ratiometric assay minimized confounders introduced by nonspecific transcriptional activators or generally toxic agents.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the design of the ratiometric assay.

claims.claim: The use of three cell lines with different truncating mutations from two different target genes minimized the possibility that drugs identified in the HTS were cell line clone or mutation specific.
claims.source: The use of three cell lines with different truncating mutations from two different target genes minimized the possibility that drugs identified in the HTS were cell line clone or mutation specific.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the experimental design.

claims.claim: A combination of well and plate barcodes allowed the pooling and scoring of over 1920 assays in a single NGS lane.
claims.source: A combination of well and plate barcodes allowed the pooling and scoring of over 1920 assays in a single NGS lane (see methods).
claims.evidence: Described as experimental method in this study.

claims.claim: Emetine and other well-known NMD inhibitors are unsuitable for human use due to off-target toxicity at doses required for NMD inhibition.
claims.source: Previous human clinical trials suggest that off-target toxicity at doses required for NMD inhibition makes emetine and other well-known NMD inhibitors unsuitable for human use (Siddiqui et al., 1973; Moertel et al., 1974; Mastrangelo et al., 1973; Tang et al., 2012; Bongiorno et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Siddiqui et al., 1973; Moertel et al., 1974; Mastrangelo et al., 1973; Tang et al., 2012; Bongiorno et al., 2021).

claims.claim: An HTS was performed to identify more specific NMD inhibitors by treating the isogenic cell line panel with a commercially available library consisting of 2658 FDA-approved or in late-phase clinical trial small molecules and natural products.
claims.source: We performed an HTS to identify more specific NMD inhibitors by treating the isogenic cell line panel described above with a commercially available library consisting of 2658 FDA-approved or in late-phase clinical trial small molecules and natural products (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: Described as experimental method in this study.

claims.claim: Emetine increased the relative expression of mutant to wild-type transcripts by three- to fourfold on average.
claims.source: Predictably, emetine increased the relative expression of mutant to wild-type transcripts by three- to fourfold on average (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Eight compounds (0.3% of the library) increased the ratiometric mutant transcript fraction more than 5 standard deviations above the DMSO controls in all three cell lines.
claims.source: Eight compounds (0.3% of the library) increased the ratiometric mutant transcript fraction more than 5 standard deviations above the dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) controls in all three cell lines (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Anisomycin is a known inhibitor of protein synthesis and commonly used NMD inhibitor for in vitro studies.
claims.source: One of these eight compounds, anisomycin, is a known inhibitor of protein synthesis and commonly used NMD inhibitor for in vitro studies, providing independent validation of the screen (Carter et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Carter et al., 1995).

claims.claim: Seven compounds increased mutant RNA transcript levels five- to tenfold relative to untreated cells.
claims.source: The other seven compounds increased mutant RNA transcript levels five- to tenfold relative to untreated cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data from the screen.

claims.claim: Four of the original eight hit compounds increased mutant RNA expression in a dose-dependent manner in RPtec cells.
claims.source: Four of the original eight hit compounds increased mutant RNA expression in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claims.claim: Treatment with all four potential NMD inhibitors restored expression of the truncated mutant TP53 proteins.
claims.source: While treatment with all four potential NMD inhibitors restored expression of the truncated mutant TP53 proteins, two of them (LY3023414 and halofuginone) did so most robustly (Figure 1D, E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claims.claim: LY3023414 and halofuginone most robustly restored expression of the truncated mutant TP53 proteins.
claims.source: While treatment with all four potential NMD inhibitors restored expression of the truncated mutant TP53 proteins, two of them (LY3023414 and halofuginone) did so most robustly (Figure 1D, E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claims.claim: TP53 has an isoform, TP53β, whose expression is known to be controlled by the NMD pathway.
claims.source: Additionally, TP53 has an isoform, TP53β, whose expression is known to be controlled by the NMD pathway (Cowen and Tang, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Cowen and Tang, 2017).

claims.claim: An increase in the TP53β isoform was observed in cell lines treated with both LY3023414 and halofuginone.
claims.source: Using cell lines with intact TP53β isoform transcripts, we observed an increase in the TP53β isoform in cell lines treated with both LY3023414 and halofuginone (Figure 1E, middle and left columns).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: qPCR confirmed the selective upregulation of TP53β, but not TP53α, transcripts in parental RPE1 and RPTec cells treated with LY3023414 or halofuginone.
claims.source: Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) of both the full-length TP53- (TP53α) and NMD-sensitive (TP53β) transcripts in parental RPE1 and RPTec cells treated with LY3023414 or halofuginone confirmed the selective upregulation of TP53β, but not TP53α, transcripts (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: LY3023414 was chosen to be the initial lead compound for further studies involving NMD inhibition based on a consistently stronger effect over halofuginone across multiple isogenic cell lines and assays.
claims.source: Based on a consistently stronger effect of LY3023414 over halofuginone across multiple isogenic cell lines and assays, LY3023414 was chosen to be the initial lead compound for further studies involving NMD inhibition.
claims.evidence: Based on inference from comparative experimental data.

claims.claim: Treatment with LY3023414 followed by whole transcriptome RNA-sequencing revealed increased expression of the mutant allele in 42% and 67% of heterozygous, out-of-frame, indel mutations in NCI-H358 and LS180 cell lines, respectively.
claims.source: Treatment with LY3023414 followed by whole transcriptome RNA-sequencing revealed increased expression of the mutant allele in 42% and 67% of heterozygous, out-of-frame, indel mutations in these two lines (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: A third of the nonsense mutations in NCI-H358 were recovered after treatment with LY3023414.
claims.source: A third of the nonsense mutations in NCI-H358 were also 'recovered' (i.e., mutant transcripts increased relative to wild-type transcripts) after treatment with LY3023414 (Figure 2A, middle).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Single base pair substitutions not resulting in stop codons were not affected by LY3023414 in either NCI-H358 or LS180 cell lines.
claims.source: Single base pair substitutions not resulting in stop codons were not affected by LY3023414 in either line (Figure 2A, right).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Targeted deep RNA-sequencing confirmed increased expression of the truncated mutant alleles relative to the wild-type alleles of the EXOC1 and SPTAN1 genes in NCI-H358 cells after treatment with LY3023414.
claims.source: The whole transcriptome sequencing data were confirmed by targeted deep RNA-sequencing of two naturally occurring heterozygous truncating mutations from each cell line. Increased expression of the truncated mutant alleles relative to the wild-type alleles of the EXOC1 and SPTAN1 genes was observed in NCI-H358 cells after treatment with LY3023414 (Figure 2B, left).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Increased expression of HNRNPA3 and LRPPRC mutant transcripts was observed in LS180 after LY3023414 treatment.
claims.source: Likewise, increased expression of HNRNPA3 and LRPPRC mutant transcripts was observed in LS180 after LY3023414 treatment (Figure 2B, right).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: No significant effects on two coding region heterozygous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were noted after LY3023414 treatment in the genes RNF43 or DROSHA in either cell line.
claims.source: We noted no significant effects on two coding region heterozygous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) after LY3023414 treatment in the genes RNF43 or DROSHA in either cell line (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Western blotting revealed truncated mutant protein for both EXOC1 and SPTAN1 after treatment with LY3023414, whereas the full-length protein levels remained present and unchanged in both the treated and control samples.
claims.source: To substantiate these transcriptomic effects at the protein level, we treated NCI-H358 cells for 24 hr with LY3023414. Western blotting revealed truncated mutant protein for both EXOC1 and SPTAN1 after treatment with LY3023414, whereas the full-length protein levels remained present and unchanged in both the treated and control (DMSO) samples (Figure 2C, D, left) (Williams et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D and citation (Williams et al., 2010).

claims.claim: An antibody that recognizes the C-terminus of SPTAN1, encoded downstream of the frameshift mutation, did not detect mutant protein, as expected.
claims.source: An antibody that recognizes the C-terminus of SPTAN1, encoded downstream of the frameshift mutation, did not detect mutant protein, as expected (Figure 2D, right).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and inference from the mutation location.

claims.claim: LY3023414 was originally developed as a PI3K inhibitor with activity against AKT1 and mTOR.
claims.source: LY3023414 was originally developed as a PI3K inhibitor with activity against AKT Serine/Threonine Kinase 1 (AKT1) and Mammalian Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) (Smith et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Smith et al., 2016).

claims.claim: LY3023414 has been tested in a number of clinical trials and has a well-known pharmacokinetic profile in vivo.
claims.source: It was tested in a number of clinical trials and has a well-known pharmacokinetic profile in vivo (Bendell et al., 2018; Rubinstein et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2017; Sweeney et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Bendell et al., 2018; Rubinstein et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2017; Sweeney et al., 2022).

claims.claim: Treatment of mice with a single oral dose of 60 mg/kg LY3023414 led to a significant increase in the expression of mutant RNA transcripts relative to wild-type transcripts 16 hr later in NCI-H358 and LS180 xenograft tumors.
claims.source: To determine whether LY3023414 affects NMD in vivo, we established xenograft tumors of both NCI-H358 and LS180 in nude mice. Treatment of these mice with a single oral dose of 60 mg/kg LY3023414 led to a significant increase in the expression of mutant RNA transcripts relative to wild-type transcripts 16 hr later (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The RNF43 gene, which harbors a coding region heterozygous SNP, served as a control in the in vivo experiment.
claims.source: The RNF43 gene, which harbors a coding region heterozygous SNP, served as a control (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: Described as experimental design in this study and shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Severe drug-associated toxicity, including weight loss bordering on cachexia and near total inactivity, precluded the longer-term dosing required for anti-tumorigenic effects of LY3023414 in both BALB/c and C57BL/6N immunocompetent mouse strains.
claims.source: Severe drug-associated toxicity, including weight loss bordering on cachexia and near total inactivity, precluded the longer-term dosing required for anti-tumorigenic effects of LY3023414 in both BALB/c and C57BL/6N immunocompetent mouse strains.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations in this study.

claims.claim: Only knockdown of SMG1 resulted in significant changes in the amount of truncating mutant transcript relative to wild-type transcript in all four genes evaluated.
claims.source: siRNA-mediated knockdown of each of these kinases in NCI-H358 and LS180 cancer cell lines was performed for this purpose (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Only knockdown of SMG1 resulted in significant changes in the amount of truncating mutant transcript relative to wild-type transcript in all four genes evaluated (Figure 3A, top).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: RNF43 and DROSHA contain heterozygous coding region SNPs and served as controls in the siRNA experiments and showed no changes despite siRNA treatment.
claims.source: RNF43 and DROSHA contain heterozygous coding region SNPs and served as controls in these experiments and as expected showed no changes despite siRNA treatment (Figure 3A, bottom).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Knockdown of UPF1 with siRNA restored expression of the NMD-downregulated transcripts, at levels similar to those observed after the knockdown of SMG1.
claims.source: SMG1 is known to regulate the NMD pathway by activating UPF1, an enzyme with RNA helicase and ATPase activity (Yamashita et al., 2001; Yamashita, 2013). We therefore knocked down UPF1 with siRNA and found that it restored expression of the NMD-downregulated transcripts, at levels similar to those observed after the knockdown of SMG1 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citations (Yamashita et al., 2001; Yamashita, 2013).

claims.claim: Treatment of NCI-H358 and LS180 cancer cell lines with SMG1i-11 resulted in specific increases in the transcripts and proteins from genes with truncating mutations, just as did LY3023414.
claims.source: Additionally, treatment of NCI-H358 and LS180 cancer cell lines with a previously reported SMG1-specific small molecule inhibitor, SMG1i-11, resulted in specific increases in the transcripts and proteins from genes with truncating mutations, just as did LY3023414 (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3; Gopalsamy et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3 and citation (Gopalsamy et al., 2012).

claims.claim: SMG1i-11 was highly insoluble and could not be administered in vivo despite numerous attempts at various formulations and administration routes.
claims.source: Although SMG1i-11 displayed considerable SMG1 specificity and marked inhibition of NMD, it was highly insoluble. While we had no difficulty getting it into solution in DMSO for in vitro work, we were unable to find a vehicle to administer it in vivo, despite numerous attempts at various formulations and administration routes.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental observations in this study.

claims.claim: No peer-reviewed reports of SMG1i-11's in vivo activity have been reported to date, which may be explained by its insolubility.
claims.source: This may explain why SMG1i-11 has been demonstrated to be an effective SMG1 inhibitor in vitro, but no peer-reviewed reports of its in vivo activity have been reported to date (Gopalsamy et al., 2012; Keenan et al., 2019; Valley et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Based on inference from the literature and experimental observations, supported by citations (Gopalsamy et al., 2012; Keenan et al., 2019; Valley et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Eleven compounds (KVS0001 to KVS0011) were synthesized and tested for bioavailability and preservation of target specificity.
claims.source: We sought to develop a new SMG1 inhibitor based on the cryo-electron microscopy structure of the binding pocket of SMG1 (Zhu et al., 2019; Langer et al., 2021). We attempted the synthesis of eleven compounds (KVS0001 to KVS0011) and tested for bioavailability and preservation of target specificity.
claims.evidence: Described as work performed in this study, supported by citations (Zhu et al., 2019; Langer et al., 2021).

claims.claim: KVS0001 stood out due to its solubility while preserving SMG1 inhibitory activity.
claims.source: Among these, KVS0001 stood out due to its solubility while preserving SMG1 inhibitory activity (Supplementary file 3, Figure 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Mass spectrometry-based assays showed that KVS0001 inhibits SMG1 protein more than any of the other 246 protein or lipid kinases tested at concentrations from 10 nM to 1 µM.
claims.source: Mass spectrometry-based assays showed that KVS0001 inhibits SMG1 protein more than any of the other 246 protein or lipid kinases tested at concentrations from 10 nM to 1 µM (Supplementary file 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 5; Patricelli et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and citation (Patricelli et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Noteworthy off-target kinase inhibition by KVS0001 was not observed until doses of 1 µM and above.
claims.source: Noteworthy off-target kinase inhibition was not observed until doses of 1 µM and above.
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry-based assays.

claims.claim: KVS0001 is bioactive in the nanomolar range and subverts the NMD-mediated downregulation of truncating mutant transcripts and proteins in NCI-H358 and LS180 cells.
claims.source: Experiments using NCI-H358 and LS180 cells showed that KVS0001 is bioactive in the nanomolar range and subverts the NMD-mediated downregulation of truncating mutant transcripts and proteins (Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D, E, Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7.

claims.claim: Inhibition at concentrations as low as 600 nM led to equal expression of wild-type and mutant transcripts, suggesting near total blockade of the NMD pathway.
claims.source: Inhibition at concentrations as low as 600 nM led to equal expression of wild-type and mutant transcripts, suggesting near total blockade of the NMD pathway (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: Western blotting showed that KVS0001 substantially decreases the amount of phosphorylated UPF1, the downstream target of SMG1 kinase activity, in three different cell lines.
claims.source: Western blotting showed that KVS0001 substantially decreases the amount of phosphorylated UPF1, the downstream target of SMG1 kinase activity, in three different cell lines (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: KVS0001 treatment of NCI-H358- and LS180-derived xenograft tumors in nude mice resulted in significant increases in transcript levels in each of six tested endogenous genes with truncating mutations.
claims.source: Finally, KVS0001 treatment of NCI-H358- and LS180-derived xenograft tumors in nude mice resulted in significant increases in transcript levels in each of six tested endogenous genes with truncating mutations, while having had no measurable effects on genes containing heterozygous coding region SNPs (Figure 3G, H).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claims.claim: KVS0001 had no measurable effects on genes containing heterozygous coding region SNPs in xenograft tumors.
claims.source: Finally, KVS0001 treatment of NCI-H358- and LS180-derived xenograft tumors in nude mice resulted in significant increases in transcript levels in each of six tested endogenous genes with truncating mutations, while having had no measurable effects on genes containing heterozygous coding region SNPs (Figure 3G, H).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claims.claim: Previous studies with non-specific or toxic NMD inhibitors have shown an increase in selected antigens from tumor-specific mutations when NMD is inhibited.
claims.source: Indeed, previous studies with non-specific or toxic NMD inhibitors have shown an increase in selected antigens from tumor-specific mutations when NMD is inhibited (Becker et al., 2021).

results.result: The authors developed a novel high-throughput NGS-based assay for identifying NMD inhibitors using isogenic cell lines with truncating mutations in STAG2 and TP53. The assay employs a ratiometric comparison of mutant to wild-type transcripts, minimizing confounders from nonspecific effects, and allows pooling of over 1920 assays in a single NGS lane. Validation experiments confirmed a low false positive rate with four of eight hits showing dose-responsive effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C30, C92-C96 describe the development and validation of the HTS assay with appropriate experimental controls and design features. The ratiometric approach using reciprocal knockouts as internal references (C27) is well-justified for minimizing confounders (C28). Validation data (C95) demonstrates methodological rigor with dose-response confirmation of hits. The use of three cell lines with different mutations (C29) appropriately addresses clone-specific effects.

results.result: STAG2 and TP53 proteins were absent in isogenic knockout cell lines despite frameshift mutations, with RNA-seq showing 20-fold and 6-fold decreases in transcript levels respectively. Treatment with emetine resulted in up to 60-fold recovery of mutant transcripts, establishing these cell lines as suitable for NMD studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C23 are well-supported by western blot, IHC, and RNA-seq data (referenced in figures). The inference that protein absence is due to NMD (C19) is reasonable given frameshift mutations and is validated by RNA-seq (C20) and emetine rescue experiments (C23). The quantitative fold-changes are specific and reproducible.

results.result: The HTS of 2658 compounds identified eight hits (0.3% of library) that increased mutant transcript levels >5 SD above controls in all three cell lines. Anisomycin, a known NMD inhibitor, was among the hits, validating the screen. Four compounds showed dose-dependent increases in mutant RNA expression upon retesting.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 describe screen results with appropriate statistical thresholds (>5 SD) and validation. The identification of anisomycin (C36), a known NMD inhibitor, provides independent validation. The 50% validation rate (4/8 hits, C38) in dose-response experiments is reasonable for a primary screen and demonstrates appropriate rigor in hit confirmation.

results.result: Four validated compounds restored truncated mutant TP53 protein expression, with LY3023414 and halofuginone showing the most robust effects. Both compounds selectively upregulated the NMD-sensitive TP53β isoform but not TP53α, as confirmed by western blot and qPCR. LY3023414 was selected as the lead compound based on consistently stronger effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 are supported by western blot (Figure 1D,E) and qPCR data (Figure 1F). The selective upregulation of TP53β (C41-C43), a known NMD target, provides mechanistic validation. The selection of LY3023414 as lead (C44) is justified by comparative data across multiple assays, though the criteria for "consistently stronger" could be more quantitatively defined.

results.result: LY3023414 treatment increased expression of mutant alleles in 42% and 67% of heterozygous out-of-frame indel mutations in NCI-H358 and LS180 cells respectively, and recovered a third of nonsense mutations in NCI-H358. Single base pair substitutions were unaffected. Targeted deep RNA-seq confirmed increased expression of specific mutant transcripts (EXOC1, SPTAN1, HNRNPA3, LRPPRC) while SNP controls showed no changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C50 are supported by whole transcriptome RNA-seq (Figure 2A) and targeted deep sequencing (Figure 2B). The specificity for truncating mutations (C47, C50) with no effect on SNPs provides important negative controls. However, the incomplete recovery (42-67%, C45) of truncating mutations is noted but not fully explained, which is acknowledged as a limitation in the discussion (C109).

results.result: Western blotting confirmed that LY3023414 treatment resulted in expression of truncated mutant EXOC1 and SPTAN1 proteins in NCI-H358 cells, while full-length protein levels remained unchanged. A C-terminal SPTAN1 antibody appropriately failed to detect mutant protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by western blot data (Figure 2C,D). The use of multiple antibodies recognizing different epitopes (C52) demonstrates appropriate experimental design. The persistence of full-length protein (C51) confirms heterozygosity and validates that the effect is specific to mutant transcripts.

results.result: LY3023414, originally developed as a PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitor with known pharmacokinetics, increased mutant transcript expression in NCI-H358 and LS180 xenografts 16 hours after a single 60 mg/kg oral dose. However, severe toxicity including cachexia and inactivity precluded longer-term dosing in immunocompetent mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by literature citations (C53-C54) and in vivo data (Figure 2E, C55). The toxicity observations (C57) are clearly documented and appropriately prevented further use of this compound. The use of RNF43 SNP as a control (C56) demonstrates experimental rigor. The toxicity issue motivates the subsequent development of more specific inhibitors.

results.result: siRNA knockdown experiments identified SMG1 as the target kinase, with SMG1 knockdown significantly increasing mutant transcript levels in all four genes tested while SNP controls showed no changes. UPF1 knockdown produced similar effects, and the SMG1-specific inhibitor SMG1i-11 replicated the transcript and protein increases seen with LY3023414.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61 are supported by siRNA knockdown data (Figure 3A,B) and SMG1i-11 treatment data (Figure 3—supplements 2-3). The convergence of evidence from genetic (siRNA) and pharmacological (SMG1i-11) approaches strongly supports SMG1 as the target. The inclusion of SNP controls (C59) and the UPF1 validation (C60) demonstrate appropriate mechanistic follow-up.

results.result: SMG1i-11 was highly insoluble and could not be administered in vivo despite multiple formulation attempts, which may explain the lack of peer-reviewed reports of its in vivo activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by experimental observations and literature review. The inability to formulate SMG1i-11 for in vivo use (C62) is clearly documented and motivates the development of KVS0001. The inference about lack of published in vivo data (C63) is reasonable given the solubility issues and is supported by literature citations.

results.result: The authors developed KVS0001, a novel SMG1 inhibitor with improved solubility and specificity. Mass spectrometry-based kinase assays showed KVS0001 inhibits SMG1 more than 246 other kinases at 10 nM-1 μM, with off-target effects only at ≥1 μM. KVS0001 is bioactive in the nanomolar range, achieving near-complete NMD blockade at 600 nM, and decreases phosphorylated UPF1 in multiple cell lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C70, C104 are supported by comprehensive kinase profiling data (Figure 3—supplement 5, Supplementary file 4), dose-response experiments (Figure 3D), and western blots (Figure 3F). The specificity data (C66-C67) from 247 kinases is rigorous. The demonstration of decreased p-UPF1 (C70) provides mechanistic validation. The nanomolar potency (C68-C69) is well-documented with appropriate dose-response curves.

results.result: KVS0001 treatment of NCI-H358 and LS180 xenograft tumors in nude mice resulted in significant increases in transcript levels for six genes with truncating mutations, while having no effect on genes with heterozygous SNPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by in vivo RNA-seq data (Figure 3G,H). The specificity demonstrated by lack of effect on SNP controls (C72) is important for validating on-target activity. The consistency across six different genes (C71) strengthens the conclusion. Statistical significance is stated but p-values should be reported.

results.result: Quantitative HPLC-MS demonstrated that KVS0001 treatment resulted in 45-90-fold increases in EXOC1- and RAB14-derived neoantigens and 2-fold increase in ZDHHC16-derived neoantigen on the surface of NCI-H358 and LS180 cells, consistent with re-expression of mutant transcripts and proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 are supported by quantitative mass spectrometry data (Figure 4A,B, supplements 1-2). The dramatic fold-changes for EXOC1 and RAB14 (45-90-fold, C74) are striking and well-documented. The consistency with transcript/protein data (C75) validates the entire pathway from RNA to surface presentation. The more modest increase for ZDHHC16 (2-fold) suggests variable effects that warrant further investigation.

results.result: In NCI-H716 and NCI-H2228 cells with homozygous TP53 mutations downregulated by NMD, KVS0001 increased TP53 protein expression while chemotherapy agents did not. A bispecific antibody (KVS-BI043) targeting TP53 peptide-HLA-A24 complexes and CD3 caused significant IFN-γ release and cancer cell killing only in the presence of KVS0001, T-cells, and HLA-A24.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C85 are supported by expression data (Figure 4C-D), IFN-γ ELISA (Figure 4E), and cytotoxicity assays (Figure 4F). The requirement for all three components (KVS0001, bispecific antibody, T-cells) for killing (C83-C84) demonstrates specificity. The negative controls (C82, C84) are appropriate. The NCI-H2228 baseline expression issue (C85) is acknowledged and appropriately handled by focusing on NCI-H716_A24 for killing assays.

results.result: In murine LLC and RENCA cells, six of twelve genes with truncating mutations and five of six genes with expression controlled by NMD showed significantly increased RNA following in vitro KVS0001 treatment.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 is supported by qPCR data (Figure 5A,B). The demonstration that KVS0001 works in murine cells is important for subsequent in vivo experiments. However, the incomplete response (50% of truncating mutation genes) is consistent with observations in human cells and remains unexplained (acknowledged in C109).

results.result: KVS0001 treatment (30 mg/kg) significantly slowed tumor growth of LLC and RENCA syngeneic tumors in immunocompetent mice with only transient weight loss as toxicity. However, no significant effect was observed when the same tumors were implanted in immunocompromised mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by tumor growth curves (Figure 5D,E) and toxicity data (Figure 5—supplement 1). The dependence on immune competence (C89) is critical evidence supporting an immune-mediated mechanism. Statistical significance is stated (p<0.001, C87) which is appropriate. The limited toxicity (C88) is important for therapeutic potential. The experiments were replicated by a blinded CRO, adding rigor.

results.result: Among seven syngeneic mouse models tested, none of the three with moderate/low truncating mutations responded to KVS0001 (EMT6, B16-F10, M3 Melanoma). Of four models with higher truncating mutations, two (LLC, RENCA) showed statistically significant responses while two (CT26, MC38) did not reach significance.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by tumor growth data (Figure 5D, Figure 5—supplement 2). The correlation between mutation burden and response (C112) is suggested but not rigorously quantified. The failure of some high-mutation models to respond (CT26, MC38, C91) indicates that mutation burden alone is insufficient for predicting response, which is appropriately discussed as a limitation.

results.result: SMG1 acts as the gatekeeper of UPF1 activity through phosphorylation. Off-target toxicity prevented LY3023414 from further in vivo use, and while other SMG1 inhibitors exist, all have undesirable characteristics. The unbiased screen identified SMG1 as the ideal target for NMD pathway disruption.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 synthesize mechanistic understanding (C100, supported by citation) with experimental observations (C101, supported by data) and literature review (C102, supported by citations). The conclusion that SMG1 is an ideal target (C103) is justified by the convergent evidence from the screen and validation experiments, though "ideal" is somewhat subjective.

results.result: KVS0001 treatment increased transcripts, proteins, and peptide-HLA complexes from genes with truncating mutations. A bispecific antibody (KVS-B043) was developed to target these complexes and destroy cancer cells. In syngeneic mouse models, KVS0001 slowed tumor growth only in immunocompetent mice, supporting a neoantigen recognition mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 integrate multiple lines of evidence from transcript (Figure 3D,E), protein (Figure 3E), neoantigen presentation (Figure 4A,B), bispecific antibody development (Figure 4E,F), and in vivo efficacy (Figure 5D,E) experiments. The dependence on immune competence (C107-C108) strongly supports the proposed mechanism. The inference about neoantigen recognition (C108) is well-justified by the data.

results.result: The authors acknowledge several limitations: incomplete understanding of why KVS0001 increases expression of many but not all genes with truncating mutations, lack of systematic analysis of splicing changes, variable efficacy across tumor types, and apparent correlation between mutation burden and response.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the study. These are honest assessments supported by the data (incomplete gene recovery in C45, variable tumor responses in C90-C91). The acknowledgment of these limitations (C109-C110 explicitly state lack of understanding) demonstrates scientific rigor and appropriately tempers conclusions about therapeutic utility.

results.result: KVS0001 decreased tumor growth in immunocompetent mice but did not achieve RECIST-criteria tumor regressions. The compound caused transient weight loss in some mice. The authors note that failure to cure tumors may relate to limitations of preclinical models.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 are supported by tumor growth data (Figure 5D) and toxicity observations (Figure 5—supplement 1). The lack of complete tumor regression (C116) is an important limitation for clinical translation. The speculation about model limitations (C117) is reasonable but remains speculative. The toxicity (C118) is documented but characterized as transient and manageable.

results.result: The authors establish the clinical context and rationale for targeting NMD: limited immunotherapy availability and response rates, incomplete correlation between indel mutations and checkpoint inhibitor response, the role of NMD in immune evasion, and lack of specific bioavailable NMD inhibitors despite evidence that NMD inhibition enhances anti-tumor immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 are background claims supported by appropriate literature citations. These establish the clinical need and scientific rationale for the study. The claims accurately represent the cited literature and provide appropriate context for the experimental work. These are primarily literature review rather than novel findings.

results.result: The authors provide relevant background on prior NMD inhibitors, known NMD targets, related therapeutic approaches, and safety considerations, all supported by appropriate literature citations.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C41, C53-C54, C73, C97, C113-C115, C119, C121-C122 are background claims supported by literature citations. These provide important context for interpreting the current findings, including limitations of prior inhibitors (C31, C97), known biology (C41, C115), safety considerations (C119, C121-C122), and relevant comparisons (C113-C114). These are appropriately cited and accurate representations of prior work.

results.result: The authors conclude that limited toxicity at therapeutically relevant doses suggests NMD inhibition may be tolerable in developed animals, but recommend continued vigilance for on-target off-tissue toxicity in future work.
results.evaluation: Claims C120 and C123 involve inferences from limited toxicity data (C88, C118). While the transient weight loss is documented, the conclusion that NMD inhibition "may have acceptable toxicity" (C120) is based on relatively short-term studies in mice. The recommendation for vigilance (C123) is appropriate, but more extensive toxicology studies would be needed to support the tolerability conclusion. The inference is reasonable but requires additional data.

results.result: The authors speculate about potential preventive applications of KVS0001 for pediatric syndromes with germline truncating mutations, hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, and other inherited repair gene mutations or mutagen exposures.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126 are explicitly speculative (acknowledged in text as "speculation"). While the speculation is scientifically reasonable given the mechanism of action, these applications are entirely hypothetical and would require extensive additional research including safety studies, efficacy validation, and clinical trials. These are appropriately presented as speculation rather than conclusions.

results.result: Different NMD inhibitors caused differential re-expression of knockout clones, which may relate to differences in mechanism of action (e.g., protein synthesis inhibition vs. targeted NMD pathway inhibition).
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 describe an observation (C98, supported by Figure 1B and supplement 8) but the mechanistic explanation (C99) is explicitly speculative. The authors acknowledge uncertainty ("It is not clear to us why this occurred"). While the speculation about mechanism is reasonable, it remains untested. This observation could be important for understanding NMD biology but requires further investigation.

results.result: The authors developed a novel RNA-seq-based high-throughput screening assay using isogenic cell lines with engineered truncating mutations in STAG2 and TP53 to identify NMD inhibitors. The assay employs a ratiometric output comparing mutant to wild-type transcript levels, minimizing confounders and allowing detection of NMD inhibitors regardless of effects on protein translation.
results.evaluation: All reviewers praised the screening method as 'novel,' 'elegant,' and representing 'an important advance.' Reviewer 1 stated 'The RNA-seq based NMD analysis, using isogenic cell lines with specific NMD-inducing mutations, represents a novel approach for the high-throughput identification of potential NMD modulators.' The editor affirmed the assay was 'successfully' executed and the conclusions are 'supported by convincing evidence.'

results.result: The screen of 2658 compounds identified eight hits that increased mutant transcript expression, including the known NMD inhibitor anisomycin (validating the screen) and LY3023414, which was selected as the lead compound based on its consistently stronger effect over other hits like halofuginone across multiple cell lines and assays.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the screening results and validation. Reviewer 1 noted 'The effectiveness of this method is exemplified by the identification of a new activity of AKT1/mTOR inhibitor LY3023414 in inhibiting NMD.' The identification of anisomycin as a hit provided independent validation. However, Reviewer 3 noted the screen 'was ultimately a failure as it didn't reveal a useful lead compound that could be further optimized' due to LY3023414's toxicity.

results.result: LY3023414, originally developed as a PI3K/AKT1/mTOR inhibitor, was identified as inhibiting NMD and shown to increase mutant transcript expression in vitro and in vivo xenograft models. However, severe toxicity including weight loss and inactivity precluded its use in longer-term in vivo studies in immunocompetent mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the claim that LY3023414 targets SMG1. Reviewer 1 stated 'The results from the SMG1/UPF1 knockdown and SMG1i-11 experiments...do not conclusively establish SMG1 as the direct target of LY3023414 in NMD inhibition. An epistatic analysis with LY3023414 and SMG1-knockdown is needed.' Reviewer 3 noted 'the authors claim that they were able to show that LY3023414 inhibited the SMG1 kinase, which is not true' without direct evidence like UPF1 phosphorylation data.

results.result: Treatment with LY3023414 increased expression of mutant alleles in 42-67% of heterozygous out-of-frame indel mutations and one-third of nonsense mutations in NCI-H358 and LS180 cells, while single base pair substitutions were unaffected. This was confirmed by targeted RNA-seq and western blotting showing truncated mutant proteins for EXOC1 and SPTAN1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these specific findings about LY3023414's effects on transcript and protein levels. The data demonstrating selective upregulation of NMD-targeted transcripts and proteins was accepted as part of the characterization of LY3023414's NMD inhibitory activity, though concerns remained about the mechanism.

results.result: siRNA knockdown experiments of various kinases showed that only SMG1 knockdown resulted in significant changes in truncating mutant transcript levels across all genes tested. UPF1 knockdown produced similar effects, consistent with SMG1's role as the gatekeeper of UPF1 activity. The authors concluded SMG1 is the ideal target for NMD pathway disruption.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the siRNA knockdown data identifying SMG1 as a key target. However, Reviewer 3 disagreed with the conclusion that the screen was necessary to identify SMG1, stating 'They argue it helped them define in an unbiased way SMG1 as the ideal target for NMD disruption. I would counterargue that this has been known in the field for quite a while.' The data itself was not disputed.

results.result: Treatment with the previously reported SMG1 inhibitor SMG1i-11 increased transcripts and proteins from genes with truncating mutations similar to LY3023414. However, SMG1i-11 was highly insoluble and could not be administered in vivo despite numerous formulation attempts, which may explain the lack of peer-reviewed reports of its in vivo activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the SMG1i-11 data and solubility issues. Reviewer 3 initially questioned why variant 11j was used instead of the more commonly used 11e variant, but this was addressed in revisions. The insolubility problem was acknowledged as a limitation that motivated development of KVS0001.

results.result: The authors developed KVS0001, a novel SMG1 inhibitor based on SMG1i-11 and the SMG1 structure, which showed improved solubility while preserving SMG1 inhibitory activity. KVS0001 demonstrated high specificity for SMG1 over 246 other kinases at concentrations up to 1 µM, was bioactive in the nanomolar range, decreased phosphorylated UPF1 levels, and achieved near-total NMD blockade at 600 nM.
results.evaluation: All reviewers praised KVS0001 as a significant advance. The editor stated it is 'a new and very promising NMD inhibitor drug' and 'an important advance for the field, as previous NMD inhibitors were not specific, lacked efficacy, or were very toxic.' Reviewer 1 noted 'The properties of KVS0001...suggest its potential as a lead compound.' Reviewer 3 called it 'a novel and - judging from the presented data - very promising NMD inhibiting drug.'

results.result: KVS0001 was well-tolerated in vivo, with only transient weight loss observed at therapeutic doses (30 mg/kg). It increased transcript levels of genes with truncating mutations in xenograft tumors without affecting genes with SNPs. The limited toxicity suggests NMD inhibition may have acceptable tolerability in developed animals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the tolerability data. Reviewer 3 noted 'KVS0001, though it was soluble and could be administered to animals for at least a month, was not entirely non-toxic, causing transient weight loss in some of the mice.' The authors' inference about acceptable toxicity was not challenged, though reviewers noted the need for continued monitoring of on-target off-tissue toxicity.

results.result: Treatment with KVS0001 increased levels of neoantigens on cell surfaces, with 45-90-fold increases in EXOC1- and RAB14-derived neoantigens and 2-fold increase in ZDHHC16-derived neoantigen detected by quantitative HPLC-MS. This was consistent with re-expression of mutant transcripts and proteins.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the neoantigen presentation data. Reviewer 1 stated 'Treatment with KVS0001 caused NMD inhibition and increased presentation of neoantigens on MHC-I molecules.' The mass spectrometry data demonstrating increased neoantigen levels was not challenged.

results.result: A bispecific antibody (KVS-BI043) targeting a TP53 peptide-HLA-A24 complex and CD3 was developed. Treatment of NCI-H716_A24 cells with KVS0001 plus KVS-BI043 in the presence of T-cells caused significant IFN-γ release and cancer cell killing, which required both T-cells and HLA-24 expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the bispecific antibody data. Reviewer 1 noted 'A bispecific antibody targeting T cells to a specific antigen-HLA complex led to increased IFN-gamma release and killing of cancer cells expressing this antigen-HLA complex when they were treated with KVS0001.' The demonstration of T-cell-dependent and HLA-dependent killing was not challenged.

results.result: In syngeneic mouse models, KVS0001 significantly slowed tumor growth in immunocompetent mice bearing LLC and RENCA tumors with high numbers of truncating mutations, but had no effect in immunodeficient mice. The immune-dependence supports that tumor growth inhibition was due to neoantigen recognition, and there appeared to be a correlation with truncating mutation burden.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the in vivo efficacy data and immune-dependence. Reviewer 1 stated 'The results of the in vitro cell killing assay and in vivo xenograft experiments in both immuno-proficient and immune-deficient mice indicate that inhibiting NMD could be a viable therapeutic strategy for certain cancers.' The editor noted the work 'slows tumor growth of cancer cell lines possessing a significant number of out-of-frame indel mutations.'

results.result: Among seven syngeneic mouse models tested, none of the three with moderate or low truncating mutation numbers responded to KVS0001 (EMT6, B16-F10, M3 Melanoma). Of four models with higher mutation numbers, two (LLC and RENCA) responded significantly while two (CT26, MC38) failed to reach significance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings showing variable responses across tumor models. The data supported the correlation between mutation burden and response, though the imperfect correlation was acknowledged as a limitation similar to checkpoint inhibitors.

results.result: The authors acknowledged several limitations: they do not understand why KVS0001 increases expression of many but not all genes with truncating mutations; changes to splicing when NMD is disrupted were not systematically addressed; and treatment led to decreased tumor growth but not tumor regressions meeting RECIST criteria.
results.evaluation: Reviewers appreciated the authors' acknowledgment of limitations. Reviewer 1 had specifically requested that 'The authors did not address the potential effects of NMD/SMG1 inhibitors on RNA splicing' as a weakness, which the authors acknowledged in their discussion. The lack of complete tumor regressions was noted but understood in the context of pre-clinical models.

results.result: Different NMD inhibitors caused re-expression of different knockout clones to different extents. The authors speculated this may be related to differences in mechanism of action (e.g., protein synthesis inhibition-based versus targeted NMD pathway inhibition).
results.evaluation: This observation was noted during the review process but not extensively discussed by reviewers. The authors acknowledged 'It is not clear to us why this occurred' and offered speculation about mechanisms. This represents an unexplained finding that warrants further investigation.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on screening methodology (C11, C24-C30, C32, C92-C96). Both evaluations praise the HTS assay as 'novel' and 'elegant' with appropriate experimental design. OpenEval emphasizes technical details like ratiometric approach and validation, while peer reviewers highlight it as 'an important advance' for the field.

Both address screen results and hit validation (C34, C36-C38). OpenEval finds the 50% validation rate and anisomycin identification appropriate. Peer reviewers accept the screening results but note (R3) that the screen 'was ultimately a failure' due to LY3023414's toxicity issues, tempering enthusiasm about practical utility.

Both evaluate LY3023414 characterization (C39-C44). OpenEval supports the data showing NMD inhibition and TP53β upregulation, noting criteria for lead selection could be more quantitative. Peer reviewers accept the compound's NMD inhibitory activity but raise concerns about mechanism (see R3 concordance).

Major disagreement on LY3023414's mechanism (C53-C57, C101). OpenEval supports SMG1 as target based on literature and in vivo data. Peer reviewers (R3) state authors 'claim that they were able to show that LY3023414 inhibited the SMG1 kinase, which is not true' and request epistatic analysis and direct phosphorylation data. This is marked UNCERTAIN by peers vs SUPPORTED by OpenEval.

Agreement on transcript upregulation data (C45-C50). Both accept RNA-seq and deep sequencing showing selective effects on truncating mutations. OpenEval notes incomplete recovery (42-67%) as acknowledged limitation. Peer reviewers accept the data without challenge as part of LY3023414 characterization.

Both support protein-level validation (C51-C52). OpenEval emphasizes multi-antibody approach and heterozygosity confirmation. Peer reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall characterization without specific commentary.

Agreement on SMG1 identification via siRNA (C58-C60, C100, C103). OpenEval praises convergent genetic and pharmacological evidence. Peer reviewers accept the data but R5 notes disagreement about whether the screen was necessary to identify SMG1, stating 'this has been known in the field for quite a while.'

Agreement on SMG1i-11 validation and solubility issues (C61-C63, C102). Both accept the data and acknowledge formulation problems that motivated KVS0001 development. Peer reviewers initially questioned variant selection but this was addressed in revisions.

Strong agreement on KVS0001 characterization (C64-C70, C104). Both evaluations praise KVS0001 as a significant advance. OpenEval details specificity data and mechanistic validation. Peer reviewers call it 'a new and very promising NMD inhibitor drug' and 'an important advance for the field.'

Agreement on in vivo NMD inhibition (C71-C72). Both support the RNA-seq data showing specific upregulation of truncating mutations. OpenEval notes statistical significance should include p-values. Peer reviewers accept tolerability data showing transient weight loss.

Agreement on neoantigen presentation (C74-C75). Both accept mass spectrometry data showing dramatic increases in mutant peptide-MHC complexes. OpenEval notes 45-90-fold changes for EXOC1/RAB14 and consistency across transcript/protein/surface presentation. Peer reviewers accept without challenge.

Agreement on bispecific antibody experiments (C76-C85, C106). Both support the demonstration of T-cell-dependent, HLA-dependent killing requiring all three components (KVS0001, bispecific antibody, T-cells). OpenEval details appropriate negative controls. Peer reviewers accept the IFN-γ and cytotoxicity data.

Both address murine validation (C86). OpenEval supports qPCR data showing KVS0001 works in mouse cells, noting incomplete response consistent with human data. Peer reviewers accept in vivo efficacy and immune-dependence more broadly (C87, C89, C107-C108, C111-C112).

Agreement on in vivo efficacy and immune-dependence (C87-C89, C107-C108). Both support tumor growth inhibition data and the critical finding that efficacy requires immune competence. OpenEval notes CRO replication adds rigor. Peer reviewers state this demonstrates NMD inhibition 'could be a viable therapeutic strategy.'

Perfect agreement on variable tumor responses (C90-C91). Both accept that some high-mutation models (CT26, MC38) failed to respond, indicating mutation burden alone is insufficient for predicting response. This limitation is acknowledged similar to checkpoint inhibitors.

Overlap on SMG1 as target (C100-C103). OpenEval supports the mechanistic synthesis and conclusion that SMG1 is 'ideal target' based on convergent evidence. Peer reviewers accept the data but question (R5) whether the screen was necessary to reach this conclusion, noting SMG1's known role in NMD.

Agreement on overall mechanism (C105-C108). Both support the integrated evidence from transcript, protein, neoantigen, and in vivo data demonstrating immune-mediated mechanism. OpenEval emphasizes the logical flow from NMD inhibition to neoantigen recognition. Peer reviewers accept the therapeutic strategy.

Agreement on acknowledged limitations (C109-C110). Both evaluations appreciate the authors' honest assessment of incomplete gene recovery and unexplained variable responses. OpenEval notes this demonstrates scientific rigor. Peer reviewers specifically requested discussion of limitations like RNA splicing effects.

Agreement on lack of complete tumor regression (C116-C117). Both accept this limitation for clinical translation. OpenEval notes speculation about model limitations remains untested. Peer reviewers understood this in context of pre-clinical models and appreciated acknowledgment.

Both evaluate toxicity/tolerability (C88, C118, C120). OpenEval marks as UNCERTAIN, noting short-term mouse studies insufficient for 'acceptable toxicity' conclusion. Peer reviewers accept the tolerability data showing transient weight loss but note need for continued monitoring of on-target off-tissue toxicity.

Perfect agreement on unexplained observation (C98-C99). Both mark as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval notes authors acknowledge 'It is not clear to us why this occurred' and speculation is reasonable but untested. Peer reviewers note this finding was not extensively discussed but warrants further investigation.

OpenEval evaluates protein absence and NMD mechanism (C18-C23) with western blot, IHC, RNA-seq, and emetine rescue data. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific validation experiments for the cell line characterization.

OpenEval evaluates background/literature claims (C1-C10) establishing clinical need and scientific rationale. These are primarily literature review rather than novel findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background claims.

OpenEval evaluates additional background claims (C31, C41, C53-C54, C73, C97, C113-C115, C119, C121-C122) providing context about prior inhibitors, known biology, and safety considerations. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically groups these literature-based claims.

OpenEval evaluates speculative future applications (C124-C126) marked as UNCERTAIN, noting these are explicitly hypothetical and would require extensive additional research. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these speculative claims about potential applications.
